text.LookupChainedMapSentence: In the chained pattern the hash map is slower than the original arithmetic it replaces (423 ns against 400 ns)
text.LookupConclusionPhrase: in the pattern of the matrix product it was slower than the original arithmetic
text.SeqSmallestSentence: at N = 100 the cached program is only 1.2 times faster (0.653 s against 0.768 s)
text.SeqMemoryCrossoverSentence: For very small matrices the cached program therefore uses more memory than the original; in our runs it uses less from N = 200 upward
text.SeqReferenceNote: We did not run the original library at these sizes. If its run time keeps growing with N^3 from N = 1000, our largest run of it, the original would need about 14 h 34 min at N = 4000 on this machine. That figure is an extrapolation, not a measurement. At N = 4000 the cached program needs 43 min 48 s and 0.13 GiB here, against 20 min 16 s and 0.53 GB in the assignment text, which was measured on a different processor.
text.SeqRunsPhrase: 1 to 5 runs per size; the table gives the median
text.SeqRepeatSentence: Where a size was run more than once, the slowest run took up to 49% longer than the fastest for runs under 10 s, and up to 7% longer for longer runs.
text.MpiNodesLimitation: The break-even measurements were taken with all processes on one machine. They have to be repeated across several machines before they say anything about a network.
text.MpiNodesSentence: All processes ran on one machine, so the messages passed through shared memory and not through a network. These figures therefore show the smallest overhead the algorithm can have, and a run across several machines will move the break-even point upward
text.MpiBreakEvenSentence: With 2 processes the smallest tested size at which MPI was faster is N=40, and it stayed faster at every larger size
text.MpiWinsSentence: From that size on, MPI won at least 8 of the 10 individual runs at each size.
text.MpiOneProcessSentence: At N = 2000 the single-process run takes about as long as the sequential program, a ratio of 1.03, so the column layout by itself neither costs nor gains much.
text.MpiRepeatsSentence: Every configuration was timed 5 times on each of the two matrices
text.MpiAbstractSentence: With 2 processes on a single machine, where messages do not cross a network, the MPI program is faster than the cached sequential program from N = 40 upward.
text.MpiNoiseSentence: The same sequential determinant was timed in several jobs. The medians of those jobs differ by up to 65% for determinants shorter than 0.1 s and by up to 23% for longer ones, so ratios close to 1 carry little meaning.
text.MpiBlockSentence: The table repeats the measurement for other panel widths. At N = 2000 the ratio lies between 1.85 and 2.13 for all 5 widths. The choice matters most at N = 100, where b = 128 reaches 1.12 and b = 8 reaches 1.78.
text.MpiOneProcessWidthSentence: With one process the ratio was lowest for b = 1 at every size where we compared widths. At N = 1000 it is 1.03 for b = 1 and 1.12 for b = 128. That fits a column staying in the processor's cache while several steps are applied to it.
text.MpiReferenceSentence: At N = 2000 the assignment program needs 13.8 s for one determinant and the reference 11.4 s, so the reference used here is the faster of the two and the comparison is the stricter one for MPI.
